The use of vaginal preparation with antiseptic agents for women undergoing cesarean sections is hindered by the lack of reliable supply systems, sustained availability, and equitable access to antibiotics listed in the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines for obstetric use. 2. There is an absence of effective systems to monitor the use of antibiotics, antiseptic agents, and antimicrobial resistance in obstetric care. 3. Referral mechanisms and care pathways for women identified as needing additional care are insufficiently developed or implemented. 4. The implementation and impact of the recommendation on vaginal preparation with antiseptic agents will be monitored at health service, country, and regional levels as part of broader efforts to improve the quality of maternal and newborn care. 5. The WHO document Standards for Improving Quality of Maternal and Newborn Care in Health Facilities provides prioritized input, output, and outcome measures to define quality care criteria and indicators, which should align with locally agreed targets. 6. Collaboration with WHO monitoring and evaluation teams will enable the collection and evaluation of data on the implementation of the recommendation at country and regional levels in the short to medium term to assess its impact on national policies. 7. Recommended indicators include the proportion of women undergoing cesarean sections who received vaginal preparation with chlorhexidine gluconate or povidone-iodine, and the incidence of peripartum infections among women undergoing cesarean sections. 8. The first indicator assesses the use of evidence-based practices among women at higher risk of infection during childbirth, while the second indicator evaluates the efficacy of the intervention. 9. WHO has developed specific guidance for evaluating the quality of care for severe maternal complications, including sepsis, using near-miss and criterion-based clinical audit concepts. 10. The Executive Guideline Steering Group (GSG) convenes annually to review WHO’s maternal and perinatal health recommendations, prioritize new and existing questions, and update recommendations as new evidence emerges. 11. If new evidence potentially impacts the current evidence base, the recommendation may be updated. If no new evidence is identified, the recommendation may be revalidated. 12. Following the publication and dissemination of updated recommendations, any concerns about their validity should be promptly communicated to guideline implementers, along with plans for further updates. 13. WHO welcomes suggestions for additional questions to be included in updated recommendations. 14. The WHO guideline development process involves external experts and WHO staff, ensuring a multidisciplinary approach to the preparation and review of recommendations. 15. The guideline development group includes technical leads, obstetricians, gynecologists, midwifery consultants, and global health experts from various countries and institutions, ensuring diverse expertise and perspectives. 16. Observers from organizations such as USAID, FIGO, and other global health entities contribute to the review and validation of the recommendations.
